morph.stmt: Sikaiana is largely isolating with preposed grammatical particles and a small, mostly prefixal derivational morphology plus one productive suffix: the noun phrase is 'article noun (nq) (q) (demonstrative)' (§3) and the verb phrase is 'T/A (neg) (prefix) root (suffix) (direction particle) (vq) (q)' with prefixes haka- (causative), ma-/ta- (stative), hii- (desiderative) and the suffix -Cia (transitive/passive-like), plus nominalising -ana (§3.3, §4); tense-aspect, negation, articles/number and case are all separate preposed particles, and plural subject agreement is by initial reduplication/gemination (§4.6).

1665.dq: In addition to the tones that operate at the syllable level, pitch in Turung speech is affected by two other considerations: stress, which is a phrase level phenomenon, and intonation, which is an utterance level phenomenon.
1665.prule: Tone language: three tones (low 1, high 2, mid 3) on live syllables and the same three on stopped syllables; the minor (schwa) syllable of a sesquisyllable is unstressed and toneless. No word-level stress rule is given: Morey analyses stress as a PHRASE-level phenomenon falling on the penultimate MAJOR syllable of the phrase (minor syllables and syllabic nasals not counted), stated with hedges ('appears to', 'requires much more analysis'); word-internally he notes only the 'natural iambic structure of Turung disyllables' (first syllable less stressed, shorter). Needham 1889's headline 'stress... on the penultimate syllable of a word' with morpheme-keyed shifts (noun+case ending, verb+tense suffix, -jo, interrogative particles) is the same penult-of-group prominence computed over root+particle strings that Morey writes as separate words ('The alternative analysis, writing these grammatical particles as clitics or even suffixes, was followed by... Needham (1889)'), in a pre-tonal impressionistic notation.
1665.srule: Not mentioned in Morey 2010 (secs. 3.1.2-3.1.4 pp. 83-84, sec. 5.3 pp. 199-201, sec. 5.5 p. 216 read) or Morey 2014:651: a single phrase-level stress on the penultimate major syllable is described; no secondary or rhythmic stress.

1665.tone: Morey 2010 (instrumental, pitch tracks): three contrastive tones (low/1 falling, high/2 falling, mid/3 level in citation) on vowel- and nasal-final syllables and the same three on stop-final syllables; minor syllable of sesquisyllables 'unstressed and toneless'; tones are perturbed by phrase position, which Morey attributes to phrasal penultimate stress rather than tone sandhi (contra Mortensen 2002 for Jingpho). Stress is explicitly 'a phrase level phenomenon'; no lexical/word stress rule. Needham 1889 marks no tone at all, so his 'accent' marks cannot separate tone, vowel length and phrasal stress.

1666.dq: The study carried out on stress assignment revealed that word level stress is fixed in the first syllable. ... Spoken Sinhala also has phrasal stress, with one stress per syllable of an entire phrase, to emphasize words.
1666.dloc: Wasala & Gamage 2005: Abstract (first page of the article, unnumbered, preceding p.474: 'word level stress is fixed in the first syllable') and sec. 4.2.1 'Stress' (p.478: 'Spoken Sinhala also has phrasal stress...').
1666.heavy: Wasala & Gamage 2005: long vowels ('the long vowels in the words are stressed'). Nash UCSB WPL 17: 'heavy syllables (i.e. those with codas, long vowels, or diphthongs)'; 'If the initial syllable is CV, it will not be perceived as prominent as a CVV or CVC stressed syllable.' Geiger 1938: a in a closed syllable 'always accentuated'.
1666.prule: Word stress on the first syllable irrespective of word length (Wasala & Gamage 'usually'/'nearly always'/'fixed in the first syllable'; Geiger 1938 'generally the first syllable', even across an intervening long syllable; Nash: first syllable that has an onset). In addition heavy syllables are stressed (W&G: every long vowel; Nash: CVV/CVC/diphthong; Geiger: a in closed syllables), so a word may carry several stresses with no primary/secondary ranking stated; the stressed/unstressed contrast is described as weak (W&G) and the accent as 'rather a pitch than a stress' (Geiger).
1666.srule: In addition to the initial stress, every syllable with a long vowel is stressed wherever it stands, so a word can carry more than one stress (Wasala & Gamage 2005: /ha':muduruvo': 'monk', /ma':liga':və/ 'castle'); the source does not rank these stresses as primary vs secondary. Nash (UCSB WPL 17, verbs, acoustic) extends the stressed class to all heavy syllables (coda, long vowel, diphthong) and finds the initial stress 'at times... weaker than the stress found in heavy syllables'.

1667.dq: Based on this overview the following rules can be deduced for pitch patterns in Jiǎomùzú: • accented syllables have high pitch • there is only one accent per word • default accent is on the final syllable
1667.dloc: ch. 2 'Phonology', section 2.3.i 'Stress, pitch and accent' (subsections 1 'Pitch', 2 'Stress'), pp. 54-58 (pp. 28-32 of the 66-page chapter file, which runs pp. 27-92); chapter introduction 2.0, p. 27 for the tone/pitch-accent/stress summary sentence; section 2.3.h 'Glottal stops, CV patterns and tone', pp. 51-54, for tone, the glottal stop and the Zhuokeji (Lin 2009) report on p. 53; Appendix A (minimal pairs, pp. 68-86) for phonetic transcriptions with default final stress.
1667.prule: Stress is contrastive only on the morphological level: in verb forms specific prefixes are inherently stressed (kə- 1/2 present imperfective; na-/nə- observation evidential; nə- outside-authority evidential; a- non-direct evidential; a stressed perfective prefix marks past-in-the-future) and the verb root is stressed in imperatives/prohibitives (vs unstressed in interrogatives with the same prefix mə-); in words of more than four syllables (verb roots with affix strings) this morphological stress overrules the default pitch pattern.
1667.srule: None: 'there is only one accent per word'; 'Accent only occurs on one syllable within a word'. Unaccented syllables carry predictable relative pitch (initial L, pre-accent H, post-accent L), not secondary accents; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described.

The default pattern for two syllable words is accent on the second syllable, with low pitch on the first ... The default pattern for three syllable words is accent and accompanying high pitch on the final syllable ... The default pattern for four syllable words is accent on the final syllable ... Wor…

1667.idn: Prins describes the Jiǎomùzú (Kyom-kyo) dialects of Situ rGyalrong only; she reports (p. 53, citing Lin 2009) that the Zhuōkèjī (Cogtse) dialect, also under situ1238, has a contrast between toneless and falling-tone words that also marks grammatical distinctions, so this coding holds for Jiǎomùzú, not for the whole…
1667.exq_: A secondary pattern exists for words with reduplicated syllables, which have the accent on the second syllable with low pitch on both the initial and final syllable ... The accent in compounds consisting of three or four syllables is on the part of the compound that has dominance in establishing me…
1667.tone: Prins (Jiǎomùzú dialects only): no lexical tone; slight level vs falling pitch is secondary to a (pre)final glottal stop and does not contrast ('Neither tone nor pitch-accent nor stress is contrastive on a phonological level, though Jiǎomùzú words have customary pitch patterns that are for the most part predictable', p. 27); she labels the default prominence 'a simple pitch-accent system' whose single accent per word is realised by loudness plus high pitch. DIALECT CAVEAT under the shared glottocode situ1238: Prins herself reports (p. 53) that for the Zhuōkèjī (Cogtse) dialect - also Situ/Eastern rGyalrong - 'Lin, in her most recent work on the Central dialect of Zhuōkèjī, proposes a simple two-way contrast between toneless words and words that have a falling tone. The glottal stop is not phonemic and plays no role in tonal patterns. Tonality is contrastive not only on the phonemic level but also marks grammatical distinctions' (Lin 2009), so the language is not prosodically uniform; this record codes Jiǎomùzú as described by Prins.

1670.prule: Accent position is set by word class and morphosyntax, not by syllable count or weight: verbs (without enclitics) stress the first syllable of the stem (except VC verbs in the perfective; resultative -a forces stress onto the vowel before the last consonant); isolated/citation-form nouns stress the final syllable (kinship nouns excepted); a preceding preposition (n, i, s, af, d, g, sg) retracts noun stress one syllable to the penult; in discourse definite nouns take penultimate stress and indefinite nouns final stress; noun + possessive always penultimate; vocative/locative final. Souag 2014a:80 (quoted p.244): 'In general, ultimate stress marks the indefinite, penultimate the definite'.

1671.prule: Lexical tone system: Stern 1963 gives four tones (low level, rising, high level, falling; a doubtful fifth low-falling) with extensive tone sandhi and a supra-segmental intonation system; Sarangthem & Madhubala 2011 give three (level, rising, falling) with minimal triplets. Stern's only stress statements are scoped to bimorphemic sequences in close juncture ('certain classes of morphemes'; 'a small number of nouns'): primary stress on the second (head) morpheme, the first shortened and tonally reduced to a contrasting register tone; 'The majority of nouns do not exhibit similar tonal complementation.' Within the syllable, 'syllabic peaking' (mora placement in -VV/-VC/-VVC) is a quantity contrast, not word stress.

tn.translation: There are two different types of tone (word intonation) in Slavisano. On the one hand there is the normal or 'falling' tone, which corresponds to that of Italian ... On the other there is also a tone that we call – following Slavistic tradition – 'rising' ... It is really rather a double accentuation of two successive syllables of equal force or with more force on the second syllable, even if often in fact accompanied by a rise in fundamental frequency (f0). ... The tones are distinctive only on the first or – unlike Croatian – on the only syllable of the word.

1674.dq: in its turn, the position of the stress in words of more than one syllable is determined by the quantity of those syllables: all stems in Sogdian, whether nominal or verbal, containing a long vowel are heavy and bear a stress, while a stress falls on the endings of light stems that consist only of short vowel(s).

Description' (EIr online, 2016), section 'Scripts, orthography, and basic phonology', paragraph introducing the rhythmic law (begins 'Sogdian is a dead language, and the phonemic tables given below are largely based on comparative phonology and internal reconstruction').
1674.heavy: a syllable containing a long vowel (heavy); additionally 'a syllable containing a simple vowel followed by a rhotacized or nasal vowel is treated as heavy'; stems 'that consist only of short vowel(s)' are light; Skjaervo: heavy = contains a 'long vowel' (incl. long rhotacized/nasalized vowels from old V+r, V+nC: 'almost all stems with n before consonant are heavy'), but 'Not all vowels + /r/ produce heavy stems' (old vocalic r > short V+r, light: murγ- 'bird' vs marγ 'meadow' heavy)
1674.dflt: the inflectional ending following the light stem bears the stress ('whether its vowel was short or long'); a monosyllabic light stem followed only by an enclitic carries a stressed short vowel (kat-βaγ type), enclitics being unstressed
1674.prule: Rhythmic Law (Sims-Williams 1984), as stated by Yoshida (EIr) and Skjaervo (2007, p. 10): the accent 'lay on the first long vowel of the word if it had one'; if that first long vowel is in the stem the word is stem-accented ('heavy stem'); if the stem has no long vowel the accent falls on the ending, 'whether its vowel was short or long' ('light stem'). Heavy = long vowel; a vowel + rhotacized/nasal vowel (old V+r, V+nC) also counts as heavy (Yoshida: maərγ 'forest', kaṃθ 'city'), but old vocalic r stems (mərγ- 'bird', kirm-, purn-) stay light; old diphthongs ai/au were possibly already simple long vowels by the Manichean stage (Skjaervo). Post-tonic final short vowels were lost in heavy-stem words (hence the reduced heavy declension). Prosody is reconstructed ('only inferred from the rhythmic law', Yoshida), and Skjaervo notes Brahmi-script evidence that the long/short difference 'may not be in quantity but in quality'.

The latter claim has been proven to be inaccurate by instrumental and statistical data (Horo, 2017; Horo et al., 2020) for disyllabic words of any structure (underived, inflected). The former view of Gidugu is currently being subjected to rigorous testing

What we can conclude from this preliminary investigation is that all disyllabic words in Sora have prominence on the second syllable ... intensity is the most consistent cue of prominence and is found on the second syllable. Duration, on the other hand, appears to delimit the last syllable ... there may be morphemic overrides to these general patterns

1677.prule: Second syllable in disyllabic words, per the modern instrumental work (b), which names and disputes the only full grammar (a); no position is given for longer words. (a) Ramamurti (Gidugu) 1931, Ganjam/Parlakimedi Sora, impressionistic: stress weak, 'very difficult to determine the position of stress in every word'; tentative morphology-keyed rules (negative ad-, causative ab-, participial an- stressed; 3sg past -'eten stressed on its first syllable; second member of compounds and reduplicant stressed; root stressed in infixed derivatives; negative don stressed; nominalizer -en/-an, plural e-, genitive o-, connective/defining e-, infixes unstressed; long-vowel second syllable after short first 'in some words'); elsewhere '(12) Generally the first syllable'; some pairs distinguished by accent shift. (b) Horo & Sarmah 2015 / Horo 2017 / Horo et al. 2020 / Horo & Anderson 2021 / Horo et al. 2023 (Assam tea-garden Sora, four sites, plus Raiguda, Odisha; instrumental, words in isolation and in unaccented and quasi-focal frames): 'all disyllabic words in Sora have prominence on the second syllable' by duration, intensity and f0, 'for disyllabic words of any structure (underived, inflected)', explicitly not quantity-sensitive and not trochaic (contra Donegan & Stampe 1983, 2004) and with Gidugu's morphological conditioning 'currently being subjected to rigorous testing'; in trisyllabic and tetrasyllabic nouns and verbs the cues split -- intensity peaks on the second syllable in all contexts, duration on the final syllable (read as a boundary marker), f0 on the third/penult or final syllable -- results called 'preliminary', with possible 'morphemic overrides'; p-word = g-word for the 3-4 syllable forms tested; 5-9 syllable forms not yet analysed.
1677.srule: Exists, placement not stated. Ramamurti 1931 marks secondary stress with a low stroke ('Secondary stress may be marked thus:,ab-jum'e:te:n,pərəgə'dab-ən') but gives no rule; in his examples and paradigms the mark falls on verbal prefixes his rules list as stress-bearing (causative ab-, negative ad-/an-/as-, ag-) when main stress is on the following root/suffix syllable (ab-'jer-a:,an-'il-le,ad-'der-n-e). Not mentioned in Horo et al. 2023 (secs. 1-8, pp. 144-166), Horo 2017 (secs. 3.4, 6.4) or Horo & Sarmah 2015, which report a single prominence peak in 2-4-syllable words.

undet.detail: Second syllable (peninitial; the authors' 'iambic' word stress). Established instrumentally and stated without exception for disyllables, the minimal and commonest word shape, 'of any structure (underived, inflected)', in Assam Sora (four sites) and homeland Odisha Sora (Raiguda, Rayagada; Gajapati villages): duration, intensity and f0 all peak on syllable 2, first-syllable vowels reduced…

1677.cfw: Ramamurti's 1931 manual tentatively put stress "generally" on the first syllable while admitting the position was very hard to hear, but every acoustic study since (Horo and Sarmah 2015, Horo 2017 on both Assam and Orissa Sora, Horo et al. 2020, Horo and Anderson 2021, Horo et al. 2023) measures the second syllable of a disyllable as the prominent one on duration, pitch and intensity, so the iambic reading wins even though all the instrumental evidence comes from one research group.

1678.dq: In each word, one stress is more prominent than the others (specifically, it has a greater amplitude and longer duration). This is indicated here as primary stress [ˈ]. ... its patterning does suggest that both Sorbung feet and prosodic words are right-headed.
1678.dloc: sec. 2.1 Stress, pp. 73-75 (full PDF of JSEALS 4(1) via the Internet Archive, saved)
1678.prule: Iambic (right-headed) stress assigned cyclically with reference to morphology: the last ROOT syllable of the (compound) stem is stressed, derivational/case suffixes do not count and do not shift stress, one class of suffixes (incl. obligatory final mood suffixes) is always stressed and another (incl. case suffixes) never; minor (Cə) syllables never stressed; no two consecutive unstressed syllables (secondary stresses on earlier roots). Not computable from syllable count alone.
1678.srule: Stresses other than the most prominent one are secondary [ˌ], placed cyclically by morphology: earlier root syllables of compound stems keep a secondary stress unless reduced immediately before the head, no two consecutive unstressed syllables being tolerated (cubˌlaaˈmíi, ʔə-ˌŋaa-ˈmíi, ˌkèe-məˈtóo, ˌkeè-məˌjúum-ˈràa, məˌkʰáa-ˈruu), and always-stressed suffixes after the root bear secondary stress (ˈloog-ˌoo 'big-DECL'); primary vs secondary never contrastive.
1678.quote: All of these correlates point to a general iambic pattern of stress. This is not to say, however, that Sorbung stress is predictable without reference to morphological structure. The following general principles seem to hold: 1. Minor syllables are never stressed. This may be due to the fact that the vowels in these syllables are epenthetic. 2. The last root syllable in a compound stem, not counting derivational suffixes, is stressed. 3. Two consecutive unstressed syllables are not tolerated. 4. tn.quote: Tone is contrastive in Sorbung, but the lexical load born by tonal contrasts is relatively low ... Sorbung has three contrasting tones, which we will refer to as H, L, and M. These are indicated in our transcriptions by diacritics on the first vowel of a rhyme: acute (x́), grave (x̀), or no diacritic (x), for H, L, and M, respectively. ... First, tonal contrasts only occur on major syllables. ... Second, there is only a two-way tonal contrast in stopped syllables (syllables with a stop coda) but a three-way contrast in major syllables of other types.

tn.note: Three tones (H, M, L) on major syllables only, two in stop-final syllables; low functional load and the authors call the inventory tentative; tones also differ in voice quality; word stress separate. 1681.heavy: 'long' syllable = one with a long or half-long vowel; 'short' syllable = short vowel (closed short-vowel syllables such as -kur, -tun in Adkur, cattun count as short)
1681.dflt: disyllables with two short (or two long) syllables: 'even' stress, no single prominence; 3+ syllables: penult
1681.prule: Awankari (Southern Hindko) word stress per Bahri 1963 XII.4: words of three or more syllables stress the penult 'unconditionally and without exception' (trisyllables the second syllable, quadrisyllables the third; 'the antepenultimate in Awankari is always short'). Disyllables are decided by vowel length: short + long -> prominent final stress (i'mán 'faith', o'gás 'sky', su'ná 'tell'); long + short -> slight initial stress; long + long or short + short -> 'even' stress (no single prominence; 'disyllabic single words may or may not have a stress'). Stress coexists with lexical tone; 'Syllables uttered with high tone are always stressed'.
1681.srule: No word-level secondary stress described in Bahri 1963 sec. XII.4 (pp. 202-207 read): 'secondary stress' is used only of sentences ('In sentences there is at least one stressed syllable with a secondary stress in some following syllable', XII.4.vi); within words only 'The weakest syllable is before the strongest one'. Bashir & Conners 2019: 49, relaying Varma 1936: 92 for 'Lahnda': 'only one primary word stress; secondary word stress is not found'.

1681.tone: Panjabi-type lexical tone coexists with stress. Bahri 1963 (Awankari): falling and high tones; 'Syllables uttered with high tone are always stressed', a toned syllable in unstressed position 'loses its pitch to a great extent'. Awan 1974 (Peshawar City dialect, same glottocode): two-term tone system (T1 mostly a fall, T2 mostly level on the phrase-final syllable) stated as a property of the verbal phrase; the thesis is scoped to tone and says nothing about stress (A's quote from it verified verbatim). Bashir & Conners 2019 fn. 17: Awankari and Kohat Hindko lack the Panjabi low-rising tone, Peshawar has it 'to a certain extent'.

1682.dq: §3.5.3 has separate subsections 'Word stress' and 'Phrase level stress': 'The main stress is always on the first syllable in South Saami.' ... 'Phrase level stress: The same stress patterns are found on phrase level as in a phonological word. In statements, the first half of the phrase usually shows greater intensity than the second half.'
1682.dloc: §2.1 Phonology (overview) pp. 51-52; §3.2 p. 72 (feet); §3.5.3 'Stress' pp. 95-96; also §6 (verb allomorphy) and compounds chapter for secondary stress on the penult of quadrisyllables
1682.prule: Primary stress fixed on the word-initial syllable (quantity-insensitive); disyllables trochaic, trisyllables dactylic.
1682.srule: Words of more than three syllables consist of more than one foot and 'the first syllable of the second foot receives a secondary stress' (Sec. 3.5.3 p.96; /luhketaejja/ with secondary on syllable 3, the V-1 of the second foot; p.195 "staa.ke.,di-bie; p.199 vaes.tie.di.bie 'receives a secondary stress on the third syllable'). The overview (p.52) states it generally as 'Words with more than three syllables receive a secondary stress on the penultimate syllable', and Sec. 6 (p.199 "vae.stie.,de+me; p.206 the -mme participles) and Sec. 17.2 (p.384 ["kaerja,koeti:]) use the penult wording for quadrisyllabic forms, where the two formulations coincide (syllable 3). For five-syllable words they diverge: p.92 says words of more than three syllables 'are combinations of the possible feet (trochaic disyllabic or dactylic trisyllabic)' and Table 3.40 (p.93) parses them by morphological make-up as 2+3 (/luh.ke+taej.je.se/ 'teacher.ILL.SG') or 3+2 (/sup.tses.te+mi.ni: 'talk.PROG'), so the foot-based rule gives syllable 3 or 4 while the p.52 wording gives the penult; the source prints no stress marks on forms of five or more syllables, so the rule string codes the stated secondary at length 4 only and leaves lengths 5+ uncoded. Disyllables (trochaic) and trisyllables (dactylic) form a single foot with no secondary stress.

morph.rootq: "The main stress is always on the first syllable in South Saami. The peak of intensity is on the vowel V-1." (§3.5.3, p.95); "In words longer than three syllables, which consist of more than one foot, the first syllable of the second foot receives a secondary stress." (p.96); cf. §2.1 p.51-52 "Stress is fixed and always word initial (trochaic). Words with more than three syllables receive a secondary stress on the penultimate syllable." The statement is purely word/foot-based; roots, stems and suffixes are not mentioned (suffix allomorphy -be/-bie is explained by secondary stress position, §6.3.1 p.195, not the reverse).
morph.elicq: "Stress is manifested by a combination of intensity, duration and pitch in South Saami. Intensity was identified as the primary feature. ... Examples for disyllabic ([kuə.liə] 'fish' and [piənə] 'dog'), trisyllabic ([kɑːməkə] 'shoe') and quadrisyllabic words ([luhkətæjːɑ] 'woman') are given in Figure 3.8. All words are produced in isolation. The blue line indicates pitch and the yellow line indicates intensity." (§3.5.3, pp.95-96; spectrogram figures 3.8-3.10, the latter two for phrase-level stress).
morph.stmt: "The morphology is mainly agglutinative with fusional elements. South Saami almost exclusively uses suffixes." (Ch.2, p.51); "In principle all derivation in South Saami is carried out by suffixes; exceptions are some less frequent derivations that involve stem alternations (umlaut) and the negative prefix ov- 'un-' which occurs with adjectives" (§17.1, p.371) -- that prefix being "a loan from the neighbouring languages Swedish (o-) and Norwegian (u-)" (§16.3.4, p.365).

1682.exc_quote: Stress is fixed and always word initial (trochaic). (p. 51-52) | The main stress is always on the first syllable in South Saami. (p. 95) | the first syllable ... (V-1), which always bears the main stress of a word (p. 76). No exception, loanword class or lexical set with non-initial primary stress is mentioned anywhere in the phonology chapter; loanwords are discussed only for aspiration, /r/-stems and vowel alternation.
1682.sec_rule: In words of more than three syllables (more than one foot), the first syllable of the second foot carries a secondary stress, e.g. /luhketæjja/ 'teacher' with secondary stress on the third syllable; elsewhere worded as 'a secondary stress on the penultimate syllable' of quadrisyllabic forms ("ståå.ke.ˌdi-bie 'we play', gärja-gåetie ["kærjaˌkoeti:] 'library'). Disyllables (trochaic) and trisyllables (dactylic) have no secondary stress; no stress marks are given for words of five or more syllables.
1682.sec_quote: [p.96] In words longer than three syllables, which consist of more than one foot, the first syllable of the second foot receives a secondary stress. This can be seen in the second peak of the yellow line in /luhketæjja/, which has a secondary stress on /æ/, that is, the vowel V-1 of the second foot. [p.52] Words with more than three syllables receive a secondary stress on the penultimate syllable.

1683.tone: Evans treats SQ prosody as tone/pitch accent, not stress: Taoping (six tones) and Longxi (L/H plus three minor tones) have full lexical tone systems (Taoping major tones 'may all co-occur in any order'; Longxi and Taoping allow multiple highs in a word; Taoping 13 and 51 and Longxi Mid-Rising occur mainly on Mandarin loans, Taoping 241 is native, voiced initials only, no borrowings); Mianchi has a culminative H accent (max one per native word, 'the accent may occur on any syllable', accent sandhi 'complex and unpredictable') with contour tones on the remaining ~5% of the vocabulary: Low-Rising 3.5% (all initials; a 'home-grown' tone sharing an origin with Taoping 241, onto which Chinese loans (at least 27.2% of Mianchi LR) and coalesced syllables have been grafted), High-Falling 1.2% (verb(-phrase)-final only, a 'morphological tone'), Mid-Rising 0.01% (borrowings and coalescence). Heihu, grouped with Mianchi as pitch accent in the abstract, uses tones to distinguish Chinese borrowings and 'has not developed its own tones'; whether its native vocabulary has pitch accent needs 'more data'. Word stress is attributed only to Northern Qiang ('(mostly) trochaic', a few minimal pairs by stress) and to a reconstructed earlier stage of SQ ('SQ dialects would also have had lexical stress at the time that they separated from Northern Qiang'); the LH>HL skew in disyllables is offered as 'merely suggestive' evidence of former iambic stress.

1688.prule: No word-stress placement rule is stated for Skidegate in any reached source. Enrico 1998 (the fullest Skidegate fieldworker): Skidegate has 'a simple level-tone system precisely like Masset Haida' with very low functional load; default tone is weight-predictable (heavy rhyme = more than one voiced segment -> unmarked high; light -> unmarked low) with lexically marked exceptions (k'a 'small' marked high; Xaayda 'Haida' marked low); the only stress he describes is utterance-level main stress, which must fall on a high-toned syllable and lengthens its rhyme. Hori 1996: pitch (high/mid/low) is predictable from syllable structure (high on /VV(C), VR(C)/ rhymes) and 'stress seems subsidiary to pitch'. Sapir 1923: per-word accent 'generally' initial but not always, shifting with rhythm, and suspected to be 'primarily a matter of relatively high pitch'. Hence a tone (Enrico) / predictable-pitch (Hori) system with stress derivative of pitch and no word-level stress rule.

Hori 1996: treats pitch as phonetic/predictable (three surface levels from syllable structure) and stress as 'subsidiary to pitch' (high- or low-pitched syllables tend to be stressed, mid not). Sapir 1923 already suspected 'what I have been making stress... is... primarily a matter of relatively high pitch'. Enrico's Masset word-stress rule (main stress on last high-toned syllable, else final; Enrico 1991:111ff via de Lacy 2002/2007, coded weight-sensitive with a fixed default for nort2938) is NOT stated for Skidegate in any reached source; 'precisely like Masset' is said of the tone system only.
